visible.summary:
Colombia has one of Latin America's strongest legal frameworks — Constitutional Court legal gender recognition since 1993 (no surgery required, based on self-recognition), "trans" and "non-binary" ID markers (November 2025), a Comprehensive Trans Law being legislated (2025), marriage equality (2016), and a Constitutional Court ruling protecting a trans inmate from prison violence. President Petro's government is pro-LGBTIQ+.

But the law-versus-practice gap is extreme and violent. More than 40 trans women were killed in a single year, with armed groups running "social cleansing" campaigns (Caquetá) and posting kill-lists targeting specific LGBTQ individuals ("All will be military targets"). Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was tortured and murdered in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, with a viral video of the assault. The UN Independent Expert urged Colombia to "close the gap between laws and lived realities amid rising violence."

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Bogotá's Chapinero district is a well-established LGBTQ+ area. The armed-group violence is concentrated in conflict regions and targets local communities, not tourists — but the organized targeting is a distinctive, severe concern.
visible.tangentialFactors: Marriage equality since 2016 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The Constitutional Court LGR procedure, the new trans/non-binary ID markers, and the Comprehensive Trans Law are resident-facing; the prison-protection ruling and the >40 annual murders concern residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The US State Department advises reconsidering travel to Colombia due to crime, terrorism, and kidnapping risks; these affect all travellers.

sources.claim: El País (14 Apr 2025): the transphobic murder of Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello (Antioquia, near Medellín) — a 28-second video, viral since 5 April, shows her flailing in a creek unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands before drowning; her mother Sandra Borja: 'They killed her for being who she was.' President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities; the report notes 13 trans people killed in Q1 2025.

CNN (6 Aug 2025): killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case — in Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals ('All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'); describes Millerey's limbs broken before she was pushed into churning water outside Medellín, and frames the repeated killings of LGBTQ people as calculated brutality even amid the country's decades-long civil war.

The Guardian (30 Jul 2024): more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023, and armed groups threaten a further wave of 'social cleansing' in Caquetá — flyer campaigns announce cleansing of 'drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots'. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men; trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work; a friend of interviewee Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): strong formal protections (marriage since 2016, adoption since 2015, ID change without medical exams) versus documented killing — the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025. July 2023: the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution (a crime against humanity); UN Human Rights Committee noted concern.

JURIST (May 2025): UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination Graeme Reid concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities — praised the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality, but warned of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience: widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT individuals must be urgently addressed as killings rise.
Ambito Jurídico (in Spanish): Colombian court protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty - ruling on treatment of trans detainees.

International Business Times (June 2015): Colombia approved a rule change letting trans people change the sex marker on government-issued ID by signing a document before a notary, replacing the old route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric exams — official Reyes called those exams 'profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice'.

visible.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.
visible.tangentialFactors: The SSMPA (14 years, applies to tourists) and the Sharia death penalty in 12 northern states are direct risks for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app "kito" gangs are a direct app-user risk.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (Boko Haram in the northeast), kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: BBC (Aug 2024): the beaten body of Abujan trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. For this record: a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

The Dial (Feb 2025): six months after Abuja Area Mama's killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. For this record: impunity is documented — police response to a trans victim's killing produced no arrests half a year on.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. For this record: current (2026) official foreign-office warning aimed squarely at LGBT+ visitors.

TimesLIVE (Mar 2025): a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; the SSMPA is described by those affected as a 'weaponised' law creating a climate of hostility. For this record: police extortion and violence against perceived-gay people, with the specific bribe amount and injury.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024), marking 10 years of the SSMPA: the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed. For this record: a decade-outcome assessment of the national criminalisation law, not just its text.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Apr 2024): 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians via Grindr and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; community counters with exposure forums (one admin's alert page drawing 43,000 followers) and sting operations. For this record: documented app-based luring crime specifically targeting queer people, relevant to a visitor using dating apps.

UK Home Office CPIN on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026): same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; Sharia law in all 12 northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. For this record: current official UK-government assessment of penalties, including the north/Sharia overlay.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Sept 2022) covers transgender Nigerians fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

HRW report (Oct 2016) 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe': the SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage — it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any 'public show of same sex amorous relationship', and gay organisations, with punishments of 10-14 years' prison; the report documents police torture and arbitrary arrests under it. For this record: the scope and severity of the national law visitors fall under.

visible.summary:
Kenya is a dangerous destination for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the colonial-era Penal Code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a $50 bribe in Mombasa, and 25 trans and intersex people told CNN this kind of police harassment is "common." The Kenya Human Rights Commission's "Lives on the Line" report documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist, Edwin Chiloba, was murdered (his body found in a metal box) — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, Kenya's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The High Court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a Transgender Protection Rights Bill). In May 2026, the High Court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and the Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. "Thousands of gay travelers visit annually through specialized tour operators."

There is no anti-discrimination law and no LGR procedure yet, but the court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill is a positive trajectory.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, applies to tourists) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.localsOnly: The court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill and the 2026 LGR ruling are resident-facing developments; the eviction/arrest/mob-violence toll falls on residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism risks near the Somali border, general crime, and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Kenya (Feb 2025): same-sex consensual sex between men illegal with prison penalty; no laws on gender identity (no legal change pathway); intersex people legally recognised as third gender; LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only in restrictive civic space.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

KHRC 'Lives on the Line' (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

KHRC press release: Eldoret High Court handed transgender Kenyans a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

GATE.ngo on Nairobi Milimani High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026 (Justice Bahati Mwamuye, Petition 27 of Jan 2020): follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a Kenyan man sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

visible.summary:
Romania is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: EU/Schengen, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The ECJ ruling means EU-issued LGR documents must be recognised.
visible.tangentialFactors: No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The court-based domestic LGR regime and its inconsistent implementation are resident-facing; the ECJ Mirin ruling directly benefits EU-recognised trans visitors' documents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Oct 2024) covers the CJEU ruling that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights (the Mirzarafie-Ahi case on recognition of UK gender recognition).

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

FRA-commissioned legal study (Feb 2008) by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu: maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners — national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints; a dated baseline for Romania's protection architecture.

visible.summary:
Bangladesh is a dangerous destination for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport.

The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct is criminalised under colonial-era Section 377 (life imprisonment, "rarely enforced" but used by police for harassment and extortion) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.localsOnly: Hijra people are legally recognised as a third gender (2013/2014, a genuine positive), but there is no anti-discrimination law and no comprehensive legal gender recognition — resident-facing framework.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Political instability, mob violence/lynchings, terrorism, and cyclone/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (12 Feb 2025): prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work. For this record: lethal violence against visible trans people continues — case specifics (Rangamati, Feb 2025).

Erasing 76 Crimes (7 Apr 2026) citing JMBF's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — 'a sharp increase' continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder/attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. For this record: the current national incident baseline — magnitude and trend for a visitor assessing exposure.

Global Press Journal: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding. For this record: the 2024 regime-change inflection point where formal rights began rolling back in practice.

Washington Blade (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's ouster (August 2024), Bangladesh's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. For this record: a dated, post-coup security assessment directly relevant to a visitor's risk calculus.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Bangladesh (September 2023, updated April 2026): Section 377 ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within s.377 (ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to 'all genders'). For this record: authoritative statement of the legal ambiguity any visitor's conduct sits inside.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Penal Code 1860 criminalises 'intercourse against the order of nature' with up to life imprisonment — rarely enforced but used by police to harass people presumed LGBTIQ; hijra are legally recognised as a third gender since 2014 with gender-marker change allowed; LGBTIQ and hijra pride events have been held. For this record: the legal baseline plus the harassment-not-prosecution enforcement pattern and third-gender recognition.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Oct 2025): after hijras refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles in Narayanganj — a traditional livelihood. For this record: extortion-driven police violence against visibly trans people, including disruption of street livelihoods.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Apr 2024): five transgender/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, per JMBF. For this record: policing of visibly trans people concentrates at transit hubs — the airport itself is a documented hotspot.

UK Upper Tribunal decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal — Home Office country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues (citing fact-finding missions and IRB Canada). For this record: asylum-grade evidence of state-tolerated hostility; international-regime (asylum) source in scope by design.

visible.summary:
Uganda is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," and the US State Department explicitly warns that "the law applies to both visitors and residents." Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes (one woman described being grabbed and shouted at that she needed to die); police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has "spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people." The law also criminalises the "promotion of homosexuality," meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the AHA targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and state violence. The Constitutional Court upheld the AHA in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

Uganda's death penalty is for "aggravated" same-sex (not all same-sex like Iran; not gender expression per se like Saudi), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic state-led crackdown makes this a environment to avoid entirely.
visible.tangentialFactors: The AHA's life imprisonment and "aggravated homosexuality" death penalty apply to visitors — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app entrapment is a direct app-user risk.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (ADF in border areas), violent crime (armed robbery, sexual assault), and civil unrest affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report 'They're Putting Our Lives at Risk' (26 May 2025): Uganda's 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act — death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', lengthy prison terms for 'promotion of homosexuality' — unleashed arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings; many LGBT people in hiding, with a small group of Ugandan mothers speaking publicly for their LGBT children.

Human Rights Watch (4 Apr 2024): Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act's core provisions — including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years — rejecting public-participation challenges; contrasted with the same court voiding a similar 2013 law on procedure.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (June 2024) covers rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community escalating, per a pressure group.

The Guardian (7 Jan 2024): fear across Kampala after the anti-gay laws — a transgender woman mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false TikTok allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house; notes the death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', international condemnation, and continued political support for the law in parts of Africa.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under the 'Do Not Travel' advisory.

Access Now (15 May 2025): Uganda's anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online — digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, while the companies behind popular apps do too little; shares 2025 case research and safety recommendations — directly relevant to visitor device/app risk under the AHA.

Amnesty International (23 Oct 2024) report 'Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names': the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in Uganda — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the AHA 2023 fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

AP (Feb 2026): 'Ugandan police arrest two women for allegedly kissing in public' — two women detained in Arua after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda: the three most important problems included 'violence and discrimination against marginalized groups (women...; children...; persons with disabilities; and the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender community)' - the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.
